content.title: About
content.content: Mature spinach (Spinacia oleracea) is a leafy vegetable cultivated in temperate climates. The plant is harvested when the leaves are fully formed but still tender. Spinach has a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a delicate texture, commonly eaten fresh or after cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Spinach belongs to the Amaranthaceae family and is a close relative of Swiss chard and beet.
Its iron content is higher than most other leafy greens, and absorption improves when eaten with vitamin C.
In ancient Rome spinach was considered “food of the gods” and used for medicinal purposes.
Spinach can be grown in open fields, greenhouses, or hydroponic systems.
Leaf color can range from bright green to reddish depending on growing conditions and nitrogen levels.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Spinach provides a high amount of vitamin K1, essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of vitamin A and carotenoids
items.content: Beta‑carotene, which converts to vitamin A, supports vision, immunity, and skin health.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: Iron contributes to hemoglobin formation, while magnesium supports muscle and nerve function.

items.title: High in antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin protect the eyes from age‑related changes and UV damage.

items.title: Low‑calorie fiber source
items.content: Dietary fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Spinach contains oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: High vitamin K levels may reduce the effectiveness of anticoagulants such as warfarin.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Commercially grown spinach often uses pesticides; thorough washing or choosing organic varieties is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Spinach can be enjoyed raw in salads, smoothies, sandwiches, or cooked by sautéing, boiling, steaming, or baking. Pairing it with vitamin C‑rich foods (citrus, bell peppers) enhances iron absorption.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store spinach in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, wrapped in a paper towel and placed in a sealed bag. Use within 3–5 days. For freezing, blanch leaves 2–3 minutes, cool quickly, then pack in an airtight container.
